title: What is folklore?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore folklore as a broad concept: definitions (traditional knowledge passed orally and by example), why it is hard to define, and why it is not just backward or old-timey. They cover folk groups (neighborhoods, families, occupations, religious groups, hobbies), the functions of folklore (reinforcing group membership and norms, or overturning them), common human imagination and motifs (such as frogs and toads as tricksters and the moon rabbit), and the coinage of the term by William John Thoms in 1846. Genres discussed include oral folklore (jokes, fairy tales, myths, games' rules), material folklore (recipes, paper airplanes, decoys), folk music and lullabies, dance, belief folklore (superstitions, customs), and body gestures. The hosts share childhood playground rhymes for choosing "it," leg wrestling, family recipes, and the oldest known jokes. Closing listener mail raises a speculative question about whether the technological Singularity has already happened.

segments.title: Opening banter and the difficulty of defining folklore
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic, joke that folklore is hard to pin down, and cite a University of Louisiana teaching resource. They read a working definition and note that folklorists have no single accepted definition.

segments.title: Folklore is not just old-timey
segments.summary: They argue folklore is not limited to backward or uneducated people and give modern examples such as Snopes and the Nigerian prince scam. Emoticons are cited as verbal folklore. Folklore is defined as shared within a group, unlike a personal habit.

segments.title: Folk groups and their folklore
segments.summary: Folk groups can be neighborhoods, religions, families, occupations, hobbies or gender and age groups. Individuals belong to many groups at once, each with its own folklore.

segments.title: Functions of folklore: group identity and norms
segments.summary: Folklore reinforces group membership and group norms, and sometimes overturns them. The hosts give examples of parody and reworking traditional material, and mention the Led Zeppelin Stairway to Heaven lawsuit and the idea that artists borrow from one another.

segments.title: Common human imagination, motifs and variations
segments.summary: Folklorists find that humans across the world share a common imagination, producing similar stories independently. Examples include frogs and toads as shape-shifting tricksters and the moon rabbit motif, with regional variations such as mochi, medicine, and rice husking.

segments.title: Origin of the word folklore and William John Thoms
segments.summary: The term folklore was coined in 1846 by William John Thoms, an antiquarian who collected rural English stories such as Robin Hood. The term was later broadened to folk life. The hosts discuss the word folk and its rural connotations.

segments.title: Playground games and choosing who is it
segments.summary: The hosts recall childhood rituals for choosing who is 'it', such as bubble gum in a dish, dirty dish rag, one potato, and eeny-meeny rhymes, plus leg wrestling. They note that these rules are passed on orally and vary by neighborhood.

segments.title: Family folklore, recipes and tradition bearers
segments.summary: Family traditions include holiday customs, family stories, and recipes such as the hosts' dressing versus stuffing debate. The hosts describe tradition bearers in some Native American and West African communities who kept each family's folklore.

segments.title: Community folklore, regional customs and negative folklore
segments.summary: Local customs and festivals such as the strawberry festival and New Orleans Jazz Fest count as folklore. The hosts discuss whether harmful traditions, such as human sacrifice, still count, concluding they would still be folklore. They also discuss regional dialects and the paint color used on Southern porch ceilings.

segments.title: Genres: oral, material, music, lullabies, dance
segments.summary: The hosts cover folklore genres: oral (jokes, fairy tales, myths, legends), material (recipes, costumes, decoys, paper airplanes, paper football), folk music and lullabies such as Ring Around the Rosie, and dance. They joke about their own dancing.

segments.title: Belief folklore, gestures and oldest known jokes
segments.summary: Belief folklore is described as folklore that affects behavior, such as superstitions and the Golden Rule in traffic, plus a Jewish housewarming custom. Gestures like the middle finger, the thumb on the tooth, and the Maggie Simpson insult are discussed. The oldest known jokes from Samaria, Egypt and tenth-century Britain are also covered.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts summarize that folklore is everything and reflects shared human commonalities. They point listeners to howstuffworks.com for more.

segments.title: Listener mail: Singularity may have already happened
segments.summary: A listener named JM suggests the technological Singularity may already have occurred and that machines are hiding their sentience. The hosts comment and give contact information.
